source.title: Why Batch Normalization Damage Federated Learning on Non-IID Data?
source.authors: Yanmeng Wang; Qingjiang Shi; Tsung-Hui Chang

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own results showing that batch normalization can impede federated training under non-i.i.d. data, and that this depends on aligning local and global BN statistics and their gradients. Its experiments test training outcomes under those conditions, refining the scope of claims about normalization and training.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training loss and testing accuracy, not training classification error or zero training error. BN mismatch analysis and the stated training-loss outcomes bear on V1 only indirectly; the main quantitative comparisons are testing accuracy. Figures 4–14 provide many plotted results without numeric values in the text, so those are not extracted as numerical rows. Table 1 reports testing-accuracy values and is extracted. Cited results in the introduction and related work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study bears on V6 through its own BN versus no-BN experiment and its analysis of conditions under which BN slows and biases federated convergence. It does not test V1: testing accuracy and training-loss curves do not establish near-zero training classification error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute slowed and biased federated convergence under non-i.i.d. data to mismatches in BN statistics and their gradients. They conclude that FedTAN addresses both mismatches and improves robustness, while adding substantial communication rounds despite little additional transmitted data; FedTAN-II reduces that communication-round cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates federated averaging with batch normalization and proposes layer-wise aggregation of BN statistics and gradients. It does not test the original centralized SGD/Adam-from-random-initialization recipe or measure the claim's training classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: Data distribution (i.i.d. versus non-i.i.d. and number of classes per client) changes the reported federated performance. FedTAN, FedAvg+BN, FedBN, and SiloBN differ substantially under non-i.i.d. data.

fits_no_version.finding: FedAvg+BN reaches 91.35% testing accuracy with i.i.d. data and 45.90% with non-i.i.d. data, against a 91.53% centralized reference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Federated BN models can suffer substantial global test-accuracy degradation under client label heterogeneity.

fits_no_version.finding: Under non-i.i.d. data, FedTAN reaches 87.66% testing accuracy versus 76.01% for forward-statistics alignment alone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregating both BN statistics and their gradients improves global testing performance relative to aligning statistics alone in this federated setting.

fits_no_version.finding: FedBN and SiloBN achieve approximately 19.4% global testing accuracy despite reported good local training performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitting clients' restricted local label distributions can coexist with poor generalization to the global label distribution.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The main quantitative table reports testing accuracy rather than training classification error. The training-loss and training-performance comparisons are plotted without extracted numerical values; results are averages of five experiments. The study concerns federated learning and a single ResNet-20 CIFAR-10 classification setting for the tabulated values, rather than the claim's general random-initialization training recipe.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 3–14 report plotted training loss, testing accuracy, and comparisons across datasets or settings; no precise numeric values are stated in the supplied text for those curves, so they were not reconstructed. No training classification-error result is stated.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and the stated model-size and training-recipe dependencies are not tested.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons are not tested.
Depth degradation, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the stated initialization exceptions are not tested.
Initialization-dependent training speed and trainable depth are not tested.
Initial stability thresholds, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability dynamics are not tested.
Higher learning-rate tolerance, the original centralized architecture and dataset settings, and Fixup's normalization-free residual-network comparison are not tested.

missing.what: The theoretical BN-specific convergence penalty: Theorem 1 contains additional gradient-deviation terms, including a term that does not decay with training duration; matching both statistics and their gradients removes these terms. This is an analytical result, not an empirical convergence lower bound.
missing.locator: Section 3.2, Theorem 1 and its interpretation; Section 4.3, Property 3

record.verdict_notes: Remove both V1 verdicts. None of R1–R6 measures V1 or directly tests V6. Figures already declared in rows_left_out are not added to missing. BN versus GN comparisons also change the federated algorithm and cannot isolate the effect of adding BN.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20 and BN under federated i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. partitions, but reports training loss only in plots and does not measure training classification error, zero error, random or corrupted labels, or model size sweeps.
